📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Small acts of kindness and self-compassion can interrupt a cycle of self-criticism and release neurotransmitters that create a sense of wellbeing.

Recent findings suggest that some years ago, my daughter was beaten up at a kids’ gathering. I asked myself as a psychologist, “What happened to kindness? When did we lose it?”.

According to recent reports, I started to dig into the research. In the World Happiness Report, researchers looked at kindness as a factor contributing to happiness, and they developed a novel way to study the prevalence of kind acts. They tracked “lost” wallets to see if they were returned. They found that more people were helping strangers than was reported before the pandemic, which may be surprising.

In a recent development, other social science studies found that measurably happier people live in areas where community members tend to donate more, volunteer their time, or help strangers. In other words, helping inspires more helping.

[Download: Get a Grip on Tough Emotions].

What explains this kindness-happiness connection? In short, giving or receiving kindness kickstarts a “helper’s high” in our brains.

Research shows that acts of kindness engage certain brain networks that release good chemicals like an internal pharmacy:.

In a recent development, the dopamine from a helper’s high is different from the endorphin hit associated with running, gaming, or gambling, which keeps you wanting more. The dopamine generated in a helper’s high continues to produce positive feelings over time. The release of these neurotransmitters is especially helpful for people with ADHD who may struggle with emotional control, motivation, and stress.

Studies have shown that volunteering, even for one hour a week, can reduce inflammatory and stress cortisol responses, and even increase longevity. Volunteering is also considered a preventative action for loneliness and depression. Teens who volunteer outside their homes are more resilient and less likely to become depressed, according to research.

Sources indicate that helping people learn to be kind to themselves is my lifelong challenge as a clinical psychologist. We tend to prioritize other people’s needs over our own. But the research is clear on self-compassion: When you talk to yourself in a kinder way, or do kind things for yourself, you’re learning how to quiet that inner critic.

[Read: Self-Compassion: The Upcoming ADHD Treatment].

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A fresh study suggests that deliberately changing the rhythm of your breathing can influence how you make decisions by altering activity in both the heart and brain. Researchers from the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbruecke (DIfE) and Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin found that longer exhalations increased heart rate variability and made the brain more responsive to rewards, which was associated with bolder choices. The findings were published in Neuron.

According to recent reports, fast breathing and an elevated heart rate are often linked with rapid decision-making. Under pressure, people may become more cautious in an effort to avoid losses, whether they are making an investment, handling a tense workplace situation, or choosing a meal swiftly. Slower breathing and a calmer cardiovascular state, by contrast, may encourage a more positive assessment of potential outcomes and make people more willing to take risks.

How Breathing Connects the Body and Brain.

Decision-making has traditionally been viewed as a process centered mainly in the brain. The new research examined a broader possibility: that signals from other parts of the body can change brain activity and influence the choices people make.

The study was led by Prof. Soyoung Q Park in collaboration with researchers from institutions including the Neuroscience Research Center at Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Freie Universität Berlin, and the German Naval Institute of Maritime Medicine.

Recent findings suggest that "Our decisions are rarely determined solely by external information. Rather, our judgment emerges from the interplay between cognitive processes and our current bodily state. It was previously unknown how the conscious regulation of our body, for example through targeted breathing, could actively control our decision-making process. We wanted to create a physiological shift using a slow breathing pattern to change the quality of our decisions," explains Soyoung Q Park, head of the Department of Decision Neuroscience and Nutrition at DIfE, summarizing the research question.

Testing Whether Longer Exhales Change Decisions.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers studied 41 healthy participants while they made risky choices under carefully controlled breathing conditions. Participants followed visual breathing instructions and either breathed at their normal individual pace or slowed their breathing while extending the exhalation phase (2:8 inhale-exhale ratio).

According to recent reports, as the participants completed a series of risk-related decisions, the research team measured several aspects of their physical and neurological responses. Functional magnetic resonance imaging was used to track brain activity, while breathing patterns, heart activity, skin conductance, and pupil responses were monitored at the same time.

This combination of measurements allowed the researchers to test whether extending the exhale did more than simply lower heart rate. They also wanted to determine whether the breathing pattern directly changed how the brain processed potential rewards.

Longer Exhalation Shifted Choices Toward Reward.

Recent findings suggest that the results indicated that extended exhalation slowed heart rate and was associated with riskier choices. Importantly, the change appeared to come from greater attention to possible rewards rather than reduced concern about potential losses. Participants still responded to losses in a similar way.

In a recent development, the researchers also detected stronger activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the precuneus. These brain regions are involved in reward processing and in regulating the timing between heartbeats, a measure known as heart rate variability.

In a recent development, "Our study thus underscores the transformative role of breath-based interventions. The interplay between breathing and cardiac dynamics makes the brain more receptive to rewards," explains lead author Wenhao Huang, interpreting the results.

What the Findings Could Mean for Breathing Techniques.

The work adds to a growing field focused on body-brain communication and supports neurovisceral models, which propose that a person's physical state can strongly shape cognitive processes.

Sources indicate that park explains: "Breathing techniques have accompanied humanity for millennia across various religions and cultures. With this study, we provide scientific proof that it is a reliable and targeted method capable of controlling our decisions.".

In a recent development, because controlled breathing is simple, inexpensive, and relatively easy to learn, the researchers say it could have value as a tool for everyday self-regulation. It may also have potential as a supportive, non-pharmacological approach in clinical settings, particularly for conditions such as anxiety disorders or depression, which can involve disrupted autonomic regulation and altered responses to reward.

Could Breathing Influence Eating Behavior?

Industry observers note that future studies will need to determine whether the same effects appear in broader clinical populations, including people with overweight. The researchers are particularly interested in whether breathing techniques could influence food-related decisions, since eating behavior is strongly affected by both reward processing and a person's physical state.

"Since dietary decisions are strongly influenced by reward assessment and physical state, targeted breath regulation could also play a role in consciously perceiving and more effectively managing eating behavior," Park summarizes for future research activities.

Ignacio Rebollo was supported by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Action (MSCA) BRAINSTOM (grant agreement no. 101028203).

How to spend Christmas alone (and actually enjoy it)

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It’s Christmas morning. The street outside is still, your phone hasn’t buzzed with intends, and the whole day is wide open, with no schedule and no one to check in with. It might feel like a relief, or it might ache. Sometimes it’s both in the same hour.

Industry observers note that maybe you’re single, estranged or far from family, working the holiday, grieving, or just not in the mood to celebrate. But no matter why you’re spending Christmas alone, the day can still feel warm and full.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, there are plenty of ways to make the day your own. Here you’ll find ideas for staying in or going out, plus what to do if it gets hard.

In a recent development, if you’re spending Christmas on your own, you’re far from the only one. More people live alone than ever, and plenty of people simply prefer a quiet holiday.

With that in mind, being alone and feeling lonely aren't the same thing. Being alone is a circumstance: no one else is around. Loneliness is a feeling of disconnection, and it can show up at a packed holiday table or an empty house.

Recent findings suggest that so what makes time alone feel good rather than lonely? A big factor may be whether you have a say in how you spend it. In three studies where people reported on their moments throughout the day, time alone felt more positive when people chose it for themselves.

If you didn’t choose to be alone this Christmas, it’s okay if that stings. What you do with the day is still up to you.

Whether you’re in the mood for a slow day under a blanket, time out among people, or a bit of both, you don’t owe anyone an explanation for how you spend your day.

Sources indicate that if you’re up for ideas, start here. If you’re feeling low, jump to How to deal with spending Christmas alone when hard feelings come up.

If you’d rather stay in, here are a few ways to make the day at home feel comforting.

1. Start the morning with meditation or journaling: Settle into a comfortable position and let your eyes close or soften. Tune into your breath and the sensations in your body. When thoughts about the day ahead drift in, notice them, then gently return to your breath. Journaling is another way to check in with how you’re feeling.

Recent findings suggest that 💙 Want some guidance for those few minutes? Settle into the Mornings meditation on Calm.

Sources indicate that 2. Cook or order the meal you really want: Skip the turkey-and-trimmings unless you love them. Go for whatever you're craving, whether that’s a roast for one, pancakes at noon, or your go-to takeout. Choosing food you’re excited about can turn an ordinary meal into a treat.

💙 Listen to Piano for Rainy Days: Nice & Cozy while you cook.

4. Do a movie marathon on your own terms: You get to choose what you watch, and no one talks through the good parts. Line up your favorite holiday films, or skip the Christmas theme entirely and binge the series you’ve been saving.

According to recent reports, 5. Get lost in a book or an audiobook: A long, quiet day is a great chance to sink into a story without interruption. If your eyes get tired, switch to an audiobook while you putter around or lie on the couch.

💙 Discover ten self-love activities to improve your well-being.

It has been revealed that if you’d like to spend the day out of the house, these ideas include solo outings and activities around other people. Holiday hours often change and volunteer spots fill up, so check details as early as you can..

6. Spend time somewhere green: Stroll along a park path or trail, or find a bench and settle in for a while. Time in green space has been shown to quiet a busy mind. In one study, adults who walked for 90 minutes in nature reported less rumination (the looping, negative thinking that can feed low moods) than those who walked along a busy road.

Recent findings suggest that 💙 Ready to step outside? Try Calm’s Nature Walk meditation with Dr. Eric López to soak in the sights, sounds, and smells around you.

It has been revealed that 7. Volunteer for a few hours: Soup kitchens, shelters, and animal rescues often need extra hands on Christmas Day. Volunteering connects you with people who share a purpose, and research suggests performing acts of kindness may boost your well-being.

💙 Feeling the urge to give back? Tune into the Random Acts of Kindness meditation on Calm to see how small gestures add up.

Sources indicate that 8. Join a community meal or gathering: Many community centers and local groups host open Christmas meals. It’s a low-pressure way to share the day with others, even if only for a couple of hours.

Industry observers note that 9. Find somewhere that’s open: Movie theaters, some cafés and restaurants, and hotel lounges often keep holiday hours. Even a little time around other people, strangers included, can bring a touch of connection to your day.

10. Take a day trip: Head to a nearby town, hike a new trail, or visit a spot you’ve been meaning to see. A change of scenery can make the day feel like an occasion.

Sources indicate that there are many ways to make a quiet day feel less lonely, from a quick text to a mindfulness practice. Choose whichever of these appeal to you.

Sources indicate that send a text, leave a voice note, or call someone you care about. If loved ones are far away, you could:.

Schedule a call in advance, especially if you’re in different time zones.

Do an activity together over video, like cooking or watching a movie.

Ask for a family recipe, make it, and share how it turned out.

You can start a tradition on your own. Keep it small and simple, such as a letter to your future self you open next year or a movie you rewatch every December 25.

💙 Not sure where to start? Explore Redefining Traditions with therapist Kati Morton on Calm.

If you feel loneliness creeping in, a loving-kindness meditation may help you feel more connected. In one study, people who did a short loving-kindness meditation reported more feelings of social connection toward strangers than those who did a control task.

💙 Press play on the Loving-Kindness meditation on Calm.

Give yourself one thing to look forward to after your shift, such as a comfort meal or a call with someone you love. Treat yourself during the day with a good coffee or a walk on your break. You can also celebrate with others on another day, and it’s just as meaningful.

💙 If you’re still feeling lonely after the holiday, here are seven tips to deal with loneliness.

According to recent reports, even if you’ve chosen to be alone, Christmas can bring up emotions like sadness, envy, or grief. Here’s how to work through them.

In a recent development, other people’s picture-perfect holiday photos can leave you feeling like you’re missing out. Try stepping away from your phone for a few hours. Those posts are a highlight reel, and the rest of their day rarely looks as polished.

If the feeling lingers, try self-compassion: meeting yourself with the same warmth you’d offer a friend who’s feeling down. In a review of studies, people who practiced self-compassion reported lower anxiety, depression, and stress than people who didn’t. You could tell yourself, “This is hard, but I’m doing my best, and that’s enough.”.

💙 Practice being a Friend on the Inside with Jeff Warren on Calm.

If you’re missing someone this Christmas, the day can feel especially tender. You can honor them in subtle ways: cook their favorite dish, light a candle in their memory, or write them a letter. There’s no right way to grieve, so let the day be as quiet or as full as you need.

It’s okay to keep some distance from family on Christmas if you need to. Calls and replies are optional, and so is explaining your choice. You can mute the group chat for the day if that brings you some peace.

If someone asks what you’re up to, you could say, “I’m keeping it low-key this year.” Whatever comes up, mixed feelings included, you don’t have to push it aside just because it’s the holidays.

If your sadness lingers past the holiday, disrupts your sleep or appetite, or leaves you feeling hopeless, talk to a doctor or someone you trust. If you’re in the U.S. and need support right away, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. If you’re outside the U.S., findahelpline.com lists free local services.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re alone for Christmas, it can help to give the day some structure. Pick one or two things that excite you, such as a comfort meal, a long walk, or a movie, and let the rest of the day unfold naturally. A quick call or text with a loved one can be a nice touch, too.

It has been revealed that it’s normal to want to spend Christmas alone. After a long or busy year, a quiet day can be restful, and preferring it doesn’t mean anything is wrong. Plan the day around what appeals to you.

If you’d rather not stay home on Christmas, there are plenty of places to spend the day. Look for open movie theaters, cafés, and parks nearby, or join a community meal at a local center. You could also volunteer for an organization to meet people while contributing to a cause. Holiday hours vary, so it’s worth confirming before you head out.

In a recent development, if you’re single on Christmas, the day is yours to spend however you want. You could cook something you love, explore a newly introduced spot, or go for a casual meal or movie with friends.

If you’re feeling sad or lonely on Christmas, let yourself feel those emotions without judgment. Consider reaching out to a loved one, even briefly. A short meditation can also bring some relief. If the sadness feels overwhelming or won’t lift, speak to a doctor or someone you trust.

It has been revealed that it’s okay to skip Christmas altogether. You can treat December 25 as an ordinary day: rest, work, or do something unrelated to the holiday. If the season stirs up grief or stress, stepping back from holiday plans is one way to look after yourself.

It has been revealed that A solo tradition can be anything that brings you comfort, whether that’s a special breakfast, a journal entry, or a upcoming ornament you pick out every year. A simple tradition is more likely to stick from year to year.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

Industry News: Scientists find a upcoming layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome

📅 13 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University's School of Computer Science, the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and the University of Washington have uncovered a previously underexplored feature of Alzheimer's disease that may help scientists identify newly introduced avenues for treatment.
  • Sources indicate that the study, published in Science, found that the three-dimensional organization of the genome differs in certain brain cells from people with Alzheimer's disease.
  • To build this detailed picture, the team combined single-cell technology, spatial mapping of brain tissue, and a newly developed deep learning model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University's School of Computer Science, the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and the University of Washington have uncovered a previously underexplored feature of Alzheimer's disease that may help scientists identify newly introduced avenues for treatment.

Sources indicate that the study, published in Science, found that the three-dimensional organization of the genome differs in certain brain cells from people with Alzheimer's disease. Scientists from SCS's Ray and Stephanie Lane Computational Biology Department, Pitt's Department of Neurobiology, and collaborating institutions connected these changes in genome folding with shifts in gene activity and the organization of brain tissue.

To build this detailed picture, the team combined single-cell technology, spatial mapping of brain tissue, and a newly developed deep learning model.

"Alzheimer's disease cannot be understood one layer at a time," remarked Jian Ma, the Ray and Stephanie Lane Professor of Computational Biology who led and supervised the study. "The genome's 3D structure is a fundamental regulatory layer that helps to connect DNA sequence to gene activity. By integrating genome folding, cell state, and tissue context, we can move beyond cataloging disease-associated changes toward understanding how they fit together and which mechanisms to test next.".

DNA does not sit inside a cell as a simple straight strand. Instead, it folds into a complex three-dimensional structure that helps determine which genes are accessible and active. Changes in that physical organization can therefore influence how cells function.

Sources indicate that the researchers examined postmortem samples from the prefrontal cortex, an area at the front of the brain. The tissue came from people with and without Alzheimer's disease who had taken part in a long-term dementia study and later donated their brains for research.

The team used GAGE-seq, a technique that can measure both gene expression and three-dimensional genome contacts within the same individual cell. Those measurements were then combined with spatial transcriptomic maps, which preserve information about where gene activity occurs within intact brain tissue.

By bringing these datasets together, the researchers were able to connect the physical organization of the genome with gene regulation while also seeing where Alzheimer's related molecular and cellular changes appeared within the surrounding tissue.

A Latest Layer of Alzheimer's Biology.

"Our study represents a major advance in understanding what goes wrong in Alzheimer's disease," noted Hansruedi Mathys, assistant professor of neurobiology at Pitt's Department of Neurobiology, who directed the Pitt arm of the study. "We know the classic hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease - accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles - but our results establish higher-order chromatin alterations as a component of the molecular pathology associated with the disease, which right now affects seven million Americans, a number that continues to grow.".

Recent findings suggest that amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles are among the best known biological features of Alzheimer's disease. The new findings suggest that changes in chromatin, the material made of DNA and associated proteins that packages the genome inside cells, should also be considered part of the disease's molecular landscape.

AI Connects Genome Folding to Gene Activity.

Another vital part of the research was Hicformer, an artificial intelligence model developed to investigate how genome structure may influence cellular behavior. The model combines DNA sequence information with broad patterns of genome folding and detailed maps showing where different sections of DNA physically contact one another.

Industry observers note that using these inputs, Hicformer predicts gene activity across different types of cells. Xinyue Lu, a doctoral student in Computational Biology who co-led the research, described the system as a computational test bed that can be used to explore how changes in genome folding might alter gene activity.

Recent findings suggest that "Measuring gene activity and genome folding in the same cell allows us to directly connect chromosome structure with disease-related gene programs," mentioned Yang Zhang, a project scientist in the Computational Biology Department who co-led the research. "Across several kinds of brain cells, this paired view revealed a consistent signature of 3D genome reorganization in Alzheimer's disease and helped us prioritize regulatory regions for future mechanistic and therapeutic investigation.".

DNA Organization Becomes Less Distinct.

The researchers identified several consistent differences in the genome architecture of cells from people with Alzheimer's disease.

Large sections of the genome are normally organized into relatively distinct active and inactive regions known as compartments. In Alzheimer's cells, those boundaries appeared less sharply defined. The researchers describe this pattern as "increased compartment mingling.".

According to recent reports, several kinds of brain cells also showed fewer interactions between nearby sections of the genome and more contacts between regions located farther apart. Cells with greater compartment mingling tended to have lower overall levels of gene activity.

According to recent reports, the team also observed weaker interactions between genes and nearby regulatory elements that normally help control whether those genes are switched on or off. At the same time, some contacts across intermediate distances became stronger.

These structural differences were associated with reduced activity in programs involved in neurons and synapses, along with changes in metabolism and cellular stress responses. The researchers also found links to senescence-related programs in microglia, immune cells in the brain that play vital roles in maintaining brain health and responding to damage.

Potential Clues for Future Alzheimer's Treatments.

When the researchers mapped these molecular changes across intact brain tissue, they found that the reorganization of the genome was connected not only to altered gene activity but also to differences in how brain cells were arranged within the tissue.

The results establish three-dimensional genome organization as another important layer of Alzheimer's disease biology. They also provide researchers with a framework for testing which changes in genome architecture might directly contribute to the disease.

Future studies can now investigate whether particular structural changes help drive Alzheimer's progression and whether any of the affected regulatory regions could eventually become targets for upcoming therapies.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health. Other CMU authors included doctoral students Shahul Alam and Shike Wang and postdoctoral research associate Junjie Tang. Other Pitt authors include doctoral students Alexander K. Kunisky and Jude Baroudi, post-baccalaureate research fellows Sahar and Sahel Ghorbanikalateh, and visiting scholar Shihan Wang. The team included researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Washington; and the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center.

#10892. Growing Older on the Spectrum: The Unique Needs of Autistic Adults

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (880 w)

Growing Older on the Spectrum: The Unique Needs of Autistic Adults

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.
  • In a recent development, our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years.
  • But even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Because so few studies focus on aging in autistic adults, there is little understanding—and support—for the specialized needs they may have later in life.

In a recent development, our understanding of autism has evolved considerably over the last 50 years. Today, many autistic adults who were overlooked or misdiagnosed in childhood are finally pursuing a proper evaluation and diagnosis.

But even as our understanding has grown, we still know very little about the unique needs and challenges of autistic people in midlife and beyond, or about the supports that help most. Why? Because less than 1 percent of all indexed autism research has focused on midlife and older age.

That means we still don’t understand the cognitive, health, and social experiences of autistic adults as they age. And this lack of research influences clinical practice: Historically, clinicians haven’t been trained and equipped with an understanding of autism in older age.

An analysis of health records from the United Kingdom indicates that around 90 percent of autistic people in midlife (ages 40 to 59), and 96 percent of older adults (ages 60 and beyond), are undiagnosed.1 Until autism research and diagnosis rates improve, we won’t understand the full autistic experience, but here are the truths coming into focus.

[Read: “How Can I Get Evaluated for Autism as an Adult?”].

Autism in older age is associated with complex health needs. Compared with the general population, middle-aged and older autistic adults have higher rates of several physical and mental health conditions, making frequent and proactive screenings important for this group.

Despite the higher rates of dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and cognitive difficulties found among autistic adults, we should not assume that autism is linked to accelerated cognitive aging. Autistic people are no more likely to experience rapid cognitive aging than are members of the general population, according to research.

Industry observers note that however, one study found that about 20 percent of autistic people had highly variable cognitive profiles; this subgroup developed an old-age profile earlier than expected compared to non-autistic adults. For these individuals, red flags for cognitive decline and dementia may present at a younger age than we’d expect in the general population. Autistic adults who fit this profile may require additional help and support as they age to remain safe and independent.

Sleep typically deteriorates with age, however, adults with high autistic traits are more likely than others to report moderate or severe sleep problems as they grow older, including problems with falling and staying asleep, sleep efficiency, and daytime tiredness.

Sleep is a lynchpin for general and mental health. Sleep problems, for example, tend to worsen anxiety, a condition that is highly prevalent among autistic adults. Improving sleep quality by blocking out light with curtains, using earplugs or a white noise machine, choosing pajamas and bedsheets made from soothing fabrics, and/or using a weighted blanket can significantly benefit the mental health of autistic people as they age.

[Read: This is Why You’re Always Tired].

According to recent reports, sensory processing differences are part of the autistic experience. Over a lifetime, exposure to difficult and unpleasant sensory experiences, like crowded, noisy environments, is linked to mental health problems in older autistic adults. At the same time, even small changes, such as noise-canceling headphones or wearing a face mask in public, can help. Adjustments and accommodations such as these should not be overlooked when thinking of health and quality of life.

Compared with non-autistic people, autistic adults experience higher rates of loneliness — the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connection. While middle-aged and older autistic people tend to have small social networks, about one in five autistic adults has no contact with family or friends in a given month, compared with one in 20 neurotypical adults. Certain neurodivergent traits — rigidity, flat affect or an aloof personality, and communication challenges — may help explain social difficulties.

Interestingly, in the general population, we found that women tend to be lonelier than men. In the autistic population, the feeling of loneliness was more common in men.

Recent findings suggest that connections with family and friends seem to provide a protective mental health benefit and lead to a better quality of life. Supporting autistic people in forming meaningful relationships on their own terms and in relation to their passions and interests could be a key target for interventions.

#10891. Panic attack hangover: 12 ways to recover and feel better

Panic attack hangover: 12 ways to recover and feel better

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • It has been revealed that you’re finally on the other side of the panic attack.
  • Sources indicate that the hours (or even days) after a panic episode can feel foggy and disorienting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It has been revealed that you’re finally on the other side of the panic attack. The chest tightness has eased, the shaking has stopped, and your breathing feels more steady. But instead of relief, there’s a strange exhaustion settling in, like you just ran a marathon you don’t remember signing up for. This is often called a panic attack hangover.

Sources indicate that the hours (or even days) after a panic episode can feel foggy and disorienting. You might experience headaches, sore muscles, difficulty concentrating, or an overwhelming need to crash. These symptoms can feel alarming if no one ever mentioned they might show up, but they’re actually a normal part of the body’s recovery process.

Understanding what’s happening can ease some of the worry, and having a few gentle tools on hand can make the aftermath feel a little less isolating. Here’s what to know about panic attack hangovers, along with research-backed tips to support yourself through them.

A panic attack hangover is the period of lingering after-effects that follow a panic attack. Even though the rush of fear and physical symptoms has eased, your body can still feel off-balance for hours or even days afterward. Many people describe it as feeling strangely similar to an alcohol hangover: foggy, heavy, and emotionally sensitive.

Sources indicate that the experience can be unsettling, especially if you didn’t expect panic to have an “aftermath.” But panic attack hangovers are both common and temporary. They’re simply your body’s way of recovering from an intense stress response.

In a recent development, note: This guide focuses on panic attacks. If you’ve had an anxiety attack, which builds more gradually, read How to manage symptoms and find ease after an anxiety attack instead.

Recent findings suggest that while panic attack hangovers can happen at any time, the effects aren’t the same for everyone. Still, there are some common symptoms people notice after a panic attack, some more frequently than others.

Fatigue or exhaustion: You might feel like your body’s battery has been completely drained.

Brain fog: You could find it hard to focus, remember things, or think clearly.

Muscle tension or soreness: Your jaw, shoulders, or chest might feel tight, achy, or tender from holding too much stress.

Emotional sensitivity: You may notice yourself crying more easily or feeling unusually fragile in everyday situations.

Headaches: You might experience pressure or pain often triggered by stress, shallow breathing, or unconscious clenching.

Digestive complications: You could have nausea, stomach discomfort, or sudden changes in your appetite that don’t seem to track.

Sleepiness or difficulty sleeping: You may find yourself crashing hard into deep rest or lying awake because you’re unable to settle down.

Recent findings suggest that these symptoms usually fade within a day, although they can last longer depending on the amount of sleep you get, your stress levels, and your overall health. If they’re frequent or overwhelming, though, it may be a sign to get additional support.

The reason panic leaves a hangover comes down to how your body handles stress. A panic attack sends your nervous system into full alert: your heart races, your breath quickens, and your muscles tighten. This is an ancient survival mechanism that’s been designed to keep you safe in an emergency.

It has been revealed that the problem? Even when the threat isn’t real, your body still goes through the motions without an outlet to use up that surge of energy.

In a recent development, once the attack ends, your system shifts into recovery mode. That crash can leave you feeling shaky, sore, and depleted… much like finishing an intense workout. On top of that, the emotional weight of the experience—fear, vulnerability, or the worry it might happen again—can keep your brain buzzing even while your body’s trying to rest.

This combination of physical exhaustion and emotional strain creates the foggy, heavy state that many people call a panic attack hangover.

Recent findings suggest that related read: Panic attack vs. anxiety attack? Here's the difference.

It has been revealed that panic attack hangovers can hit you hard, and you may not have the energy to do much after. These ideas are simple, low-lift, and designed for the days when everything feels like just too much.

Pick what’s doable today and ignore the rest: your nervous system will get the memo.

Industry observers note that your body just ran an internal marathon, and it’s important to be kind to it. If you can, postpone non-urgent tasks and try to give yourself a small recovery window.

In a recent development, set a 10–15 minute timer, lie down or sit with support behind your back, and let your eyes rest. If you’re at work, try a short break, plus two minutes of slow breathing in a quiet corner. A pause can often help you recover faster.

Related read: Stressed and short on time? Here's how to try micro-meditation.

Staying hydrated and keeping your blood sugar steady can help you feel more balanced as your body recovers from a panic attack. Dehydration and dips in blood sugar can make fatigue, headaches, and brain fog worse.

Drink water or an electrolyte beverage and have a simple snack, like fruit with nut butter, yogurt, or toast. This helps give your system some fuel to reset.

Industry observers note that slow, gentle breathing tells your nervous system that you’re safe. Try this for 2–3 minutes: Inhale through your nose for four counts, and then exhale through pursed lips for six or eight.

Longer exhales can help your nervous system shift from fight-or-flight into rest-and-digest mode. But only do this if you feel comfortable. Don’t try to force anything.

💙 If you need some guidance, check out Reset with the Breath with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

In a recent development, panic can cause you to tighten your muscles, especially in the jaw, chest, shoulders, and hands. Short, light movements help clear it all without overexertion.

You don’t have to do anything too intense. Simple shoulder rolls, gentle neck circles, a slow doorframe chest stretch, or a five-minute walk around the block or office floor can all help. If you’re seated, simply unclench your jaw, open and close your hands 10 times, or shake out your arms. The point is to loosen everything up.

In a recent development, 💙 Need a little extra support? Try the Softening Anxiety Daily Move session with Mel Mah on the Calm app.

Quick temperature shifts, like splashing cool water on your face or holding something cold, can help ground you and interrupt the leftover jitters after a panic attack.

This is because it’s actually a form of grounding that allows your nervous system to anchor itself back to the present moment.

Related read: 18 grounding techniques to help relieve anxiety.

Decision fatigue amplifies the brain fog that comes after a panic attack, so try to cut down on the number of choices you’re making.

Industry observers note that trim your to-do list to one or two essentials, and choose “good enough” over perfect. Reheat leftovers instead of cooking, tell your coworkers you’re running a little behind, and move all noncritical tasks to the next day. It sounds simple, but having that space will help more than you know.

Reduce stimulation to ease the post-panic attack stress. Dim overhead lights, switch to warm lamps, lower the volume on any music or background noise, and silence non-urgent notifications on your phone and laptop for an hour.

In a recent development, if noise is unavoidable, try earplugs or a brown-noise playlist. If you enjoy aromatherapy a familiar scent (like lavender, vanilla, or eucalyptus) can also be grounding.

Writing a few lines about your feelings and symptoms post-panic attack can help your brain process what happened and move forward. Research indicates that journaling supports emotional regulation, which is why so many people find it useful for panic recovery, too — even if it’s just a quick note or voice memo.

In a recent development, consider reflecting on what triggered your attack, what symptoms you noticed, what helped calm you down, and what you could do differently next time. This can help give you more effective coping tools for future attacks.

Reaching out, even with a simple text, helps calm the nervous system. Social support is one of the strongest buffers for stress recovery.

In a recent development, send a text to someone you trust, simply asking to check in. If talking feels like too much, having someone just sit with you can also be helpful.

Related read: How to help someone having a panic attack (and what to avoid).

It has been revealed that after a panic attack, your system is more sensitive. Consider skipping or reducing how much caffeine you drink, as it can re-spark jitters. And avoid alcohol, as it’s been known to disrupt sleep and mood. Swap in decaf, herbal tea, or a half-caf and make sure to focus on nutrition and hydration to help support recovery.

Recent findings suggest that fatigue after a panic attack is real, and quality sleep helps reset your stress response. Keep bedtime predictable with a wind-down routine you enjoy, darken the room, and cool it slightly.

According to recent reports, if you desperately need a nap, cap it at 20–30 minutes, and avoid late-evening naps in order to protect nighttime sleep. If your mind spins when it’s time to go to bed, try a quiet meditation or body scan. This can help quiet the mind long enough to help you drift off faster.

💙 Fall asleep with ease thanks to the White Noise soundscape on the Calm app.

Even just knowing what you’ll do next time can take the edge off that heavy, shaky feeling that lingers after a panic attack. One simple idea? Make a three-step blueprint that you keep on your phone or in your wallet.

Spend two minutes on long exhales or humming.

Splash cold water on your face or run cool water over your wrists.

It also helps to add one contact you trust to call or text.

While you may not be able to prevent every spiral, it always helps to have something in your back pocket (literally) that helps you feel less alone and more ready.

Yes, a hangover can sometimes trigger panic attacks. This is because alcohol disrupts sleep, dehydrates your body, and causes blood sugar swings — and all of these effects can make your nervous system more sensitive the next day.

According to recent reports, alcohol also interferes with the neurotransmitters that regulate your mood, which can amplify feelings of unease or dread. If you’re already prone to anxiety, that extra stress can tip into panic.

Every person who drinks won’t necessarily have a panic attack, but if you notice a pattern between hangovers and panic, it may help to cut back, hydrate more intentionally, or avoid drinking on nights before demanding days.

For most people, the hungover feeling eases within a few hours, but it’s not unusual for fatigue or brain fog to stretch into the next day. The duration of a panic attack hangover depends on several factors: how intense the panic attack was, how long it lasted, how well you slept, and what kind of support you gave your body afterward.

Sources indicate that try to find the recovery initiative that works best for you: getting enough water, food, gentle movement, and rest can speed up the reset. However, if you find that your hangover lasts longer than 24 hours or happens every time you panic, it may be a sign that your nervous system is under strain. In this case, getting some professional support can help.

Industry observers note that brain fog and fatigue are your nervous system’s way of asking for recovery time, so supporting your body can make the fog lift faster. Start with water or an electrolyte drink, followed by a small, balanced meal or snack. Light movement like walking or stretching also helps by boosting circulation and clearing leftover stress hormones, while short breaks from screens give your brain a reset.

According to recent reports, some people find that changing environments—stepping outside for fresh air, moving to a quieter space, or dimming harsh lighting—makes a noticeable difference in clarity. Rest is crucial, too, but you don’t want to overdo it. A short nap capped at 20–30 minutes usually helps more than staying in bed for hours.

Industry observers note that the exhaustion you feel after a panic attack is the crash that comes after an adrenaline surge. Basically, when you panic, your body burns through enormous amounts of energy in a short time. Your heart rate rises, your muscles tense, and your brain goes into overdrive to scan for danger.

Even though there isn’t an actual threat, your body doesn’t know that, so it uses up its resources as if there is. Once the panic attack passes, your hormones shift, and your body needs to come down from the emotional intensity. While it’s easy to look at this exhaustion as weakness, it’s really just your body’s way of recovering from an all-systems-on alert. That’s why gentleness is key for recovery.

In a recent development, you can’t always prevent panic attacks, but you can definitely soften the after-effects. The most helpful strategies are proactive, or preventing one before it comes on. Think: getting consistent sleep, eating balanced meals to keep blood sugar steady, staying hydrated, and limiting alcohol or excessive caffeine.

Some people find it useful to have a short aftercare routine ready, too, such as hydrating, stretching, or texting a friend once the panic subsides. This helps to prevent the hangover from stretching out longer than necessary.

Industry observers note that over time, therapy and skills training can also reduce both the frequency of panic attacks and the severity of hangovers. You’ll essentially learn how to give your nervous system a softer landing.

Headaches and sore muscles are common after a panic attack. During panic, your jaw, neck, shoulders, and chest may tighten without you noticing, and fast, shallow breathing could add to the headache.

Industry observers note that unclenching your jaw, rolling your shoulders, or holding a cool compress to your forehead may help. Get care right away if you have a sudden, severe headache, chest pain, numbness or weakness, trouble speaking, or vision changes. If your headache lasts longer than you’d expect, check in with your doctor or primary care provider.

It has been revealed that after a panic attack, give your body a few minutes to settle before you do anything else. Stay where you are if it’s safe, and take a few slow breaths with a longer exhale.

It has been revealed that shakiness or fog is a normal part of coming down from panic, so you don’t need to push through it. Once the first wave passes, tell someone you trust what happened and lower the demands on yourself for the rest of the day. The 12 tips above have ideas for the hours that follow. If panic attacks keep happening, talking with a doctor or mental health professional may help.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neurodivergent kids aren’t the only ones who struggle with changing routines or fresh life phases. Adults can feel overwhelmed by transitions, too.

Whether starting a upcoming job, moving to a new town, or sending a child off to college, transitions are equal parts exciting and uncomfortable for neurodivergent individuals.

The struggle often looks different in children and adults, but the demand is much the same: Stop what you are doing, shift your attention, figure out the next step, manage your emotions, and move into a different role, task, place, or expectation. The bigger the transition, the harder it feels.

Typical transitions include returning to work after a vacation, adjusting to a fresh schedule, shifting from work to parenting mode, navigating relationship changes, and recovering from illness or injury.

[Free Download: Get Control of Your Life and Schedule].

Recent findings suggest that from the outside, the response of an adult with ADHD may look like procrastination, avoidance, irritability, disorganization, or poor follow-through. Internally, they are likely dealing with anxiety, emotional overload, decision fatigue, time blindness, or the frustration of knowing exactly what needs to be done but struggling to begin.

“I struggle so badly with transitions (they feel almost literally painful) that I spend up to five hours in a state of crippling inertia before handling a task that needs to be done,” wrote one woman with ADHD in a social media post, pleading for help.

Transitions can be especially difficult when they involve uncertainty. A new job may bring excitement and anxiety about performance. A vacation may feel adventurous and overwhelming. Even a positive life change can feel unsettling when structure falls away.

“I don’t travel much,” states Layla, an ADDitude reader from California. “Transitions are hard for me.”.

[Get This Free Download: Finish Your To-Do List Today].

Shave the rough edges off transitions by doing the following seven things:.

Most importantly, adults with ADHD should keep in mind that embracing change easily is not necessarily a sign of maturity. Feelings of anxiety around transitions may just mean that your brain needs more preview, structure, recovery, and support to move from one demand to the next.

#10889. Breaking: Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

Breaking: Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

📅 14 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1201 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life.
  • It has been revealed that the study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India.
  • In a recent development, superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life. Their findings suggest that the condition of the brain's local communication pathways could influence how strongly gray matter loss affects cognition.

It has been revealed that the study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India. The research is among the first to investigate superficial white matter in a community-based population from a low- and middle-income country.

The Brain's Local Communication Network.

In a recent development, superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain. These short, curved fibers connect nearby regions of the cerebral cortex, allowing them to exchange information. They can be thought of as local roads linking neighboring areas of the brain.

Gray matter serves a different role. It contains many of the nerve cells responsible for processing information. Together, gray matter and the white matter directly beneath it form closely connected systems that may both contribute to cognitive health.

Industry observers note that "Gray matter and superficial white matter are physically close and may play different roles: gray matter processes information, while superficial white matter helps nearby brain regions communicate," said Yingxu Liu, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the Stevens INI and first author of the study. "Our findings suggest that cognitive health depends not only on how much gray matter is preserved, but also on the condition of the wiring that connects it.".

Measuring the Brain's Hidden Wiring.

To investigate these local connections, the researchers used an advanced type of diffusion MRI. This imaging technique tracks the movement of water through brain tissue, allowing scientists to examine microscopic features that conventional brain scans may not reveal.

According to recent reports, the researchers focused on measurements related to neurite density and the amount of freely moving water surrounding these structures. Neurites are the small projections through which nerve cells send and receive signals. A lower density of neurites or an increase in free water can indicate damage or disruption in tissue associated with processes including loss of myelin, inflammation, or swelling.

Participants also underwent assessments covering several areas of cognition, including language, memory, executive function, and visuospatial ability.

The most consistent connection between superficial white matter health and cognitive performance involved language. People with healthier superficial white matter tended to perform better on language tests. The strongest associations appeared in frontotemporal regions of the brain involved in recognizing words, speaking fluently, and temporarily holding language information in mind.

Healthy Wiring May Cushion Gray Matter Loss.

It has been revealed that measures of gray matter atrophy were still the strongest overall predictors of cognitive ability. However, the researchers found that the impact of gray matter loss appeared to vary depending on the health of nearby superficial white matter.

Recent findings suggest that when these local connections showed poorer integrity, gray matter loss was more strongly associated with impaired language performance and broader cognitive difficulties. When superficial white matter was healthier, the link between gray matter loss and poorer cognition was weaker.

This raises the possibility that the condition of the brain's local wiring could help explain why two people with similar amounts of gray matter loss do not necessarily experience the same degree of cognitive decline.

Sources indicate that "The findings point to superficial white matter as a possible source of resilience," remarked Leon Aksman, PhD, assistant professor of research neurology at the Stevens INI and senior author of the study. "Two people with a similar degree of gray matter loss may not experience the same cognitive effects if the local connections surrounding that gray matter differ in health. Following participants over time will be essential to test whether preserving these connections can help maintain cognition.".

Expanding Brain Aging Research Beyond Typical Populations.

The researchers drew their data from the Harmonized Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia for the Longitudinal Aging Study in India, known as LASI-DAD. More than half of the larger LASI-DAD population has low literacy, while about 60% lives in rural communities.

Populations with these characteristics have historically been underrepresented in brain imaging studies, making the research an opportunity to examine cognitive aging across a broader range of social, educational, and geographic backgrounds.

In this analysis, the association between superficial white matter and language ability was stronger among people who were unable to read or who read incorrectly, those who had received no formal education, and participants living in rural areas.

According to recent reports, the researchers emphasize that the results do not establish that these social factors caused changes in brain tissue. Instead, they suggest that brain aging may be shaped by a complex combination of experiences throughout life, including education, social circumstances, health, and environmental exposures.

What Scientists Still Need to Learn.

In a recent development, because participants were examined at only one point in time, the study cannot establish which brain changes occurred first. Researchers do not yet know whether deterioration of superficial white matter begins before gray matter loss, develops alongside it, or precedes measurable cognitive decline.

Recent findings suggest that long-term research that follows people as they age will be needed to clarify these relationships. Future studies will also investigate how vascular health, inflammation, Alzheimer's related proteins, and other biological factors interact with changes in gray and white matter.

Recent findings suggest that "A fuller understanding of brain aging requires research that reflects the world's social, cultural, and geographic diversity," said Arthur W. Toga, PhD, director of the Stevens INI and Provost Professor at USC. "By studying an underrepresented population and looking beyond gray matter alone, this work brings us closer to identifying the biological and social factors that may protect cognition across the lifespan.".

It has been revealed that in addition to Liu and Aksman, the study's authors include Kirsten M. Lynch, Miguel Arce Rentería, Emma Nichols, Alden L. Gross, Lindsay C. Kobayashi, Neda Jahanshad, John P. John, Harshita V. Vishwakarma, Pranali Khobragade, Joyita Banerjee, Niranjan Khandelwal, Jyoti Dangwal, Sudhir Saxena, Nirod Medhi, Soumik Das, Prudhvinath Reddy, Pratyaksha Rana, Arjun Narula, Saravanan Kannan, Dinesh Patel, A. B. Dey, Sharmistha Dey, and Jinkook Lee.

The research was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG080473, RF1AG087965, RF1AG088003, R01AG087513), the National Institute of Mental Health (R01MH134004), the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (RF1NS136995), and the Office of the Director of the National Institutes of Health (S10OD032285).

How to write your retirement message or announcement at work

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • And while it’s thrilling to finally have time to do all the things you’ve been meaning to do, leaving behind your coworkers, especially if you’re close, can feel bittersweet.
  • Sources indicate that to bring a sense of closure, many people like to write a message of gratitude to their colleagues before they sign off for the last time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Retirement is the end of an era. And while it’s thrilling to finally have time to do all the things you’ve been meaning to do, leaving behind your coworkers, especially if you’re close, can feel bittersweet.

Sources indicate that to bring a sense of closure, many people like to write a message of gratitude to their colleagues before they sign off for the last time. But what do you say? How can you possibly sum up years of collaboration, chaos, and connection in just a few sentences?

Industry observers note that nobody wants the stress of staring at a blinking cursor, so here are a few tips for announcing your retirement and writing a thoughtful goodbye message to the people you’ve worked with. By adapting them to fit your specific role and personality, you can acknowledge the relationships that mattered, offer an authentic goodbye, and leave with intention. Happy retirement!

You might think that your retirement messages need to be a perfect balance of professional, funny, and sweet, but what’s most important is that you sound like yourself.

To ensure that your note is polished and professional, keep these tips in mind.

In a recent development, most people don’t want to read a long email, no matter who it’s from. A few honest lines work perfectly.

“The time has come. After 12 years of wearing the same pants four out of five days of the week and drinking lukewarm coffee from the break room, I’m retiring. I’ve truly loved working with you and appreciate every wild and wonderful day we shared.”.

According to recent reports, “Before I officially retire, I wanted to say thank you for this beautiful ride. You’ve all been unforgettable and lovely to me. You’re the reason this job didn’t feel like work.”.

It has been revealed that “After 18 years, I’ve officially graduated to more peaceful days filled with puzzles and midday naps. Logging off now, grateful for every moment. I will miss you all!”.

💙 As you head into retirement, reflect on all the good times you had at work. Gratitude for the Day with Chibs Okereke can help you tap into those positive feelings.

Sources indicate that gratitude makes goodbye messages feel a little warmer. Think about the people or experiences that left a mark, like the coworker who knew your coffee order by heart or the one who always lent you their umbrella when it was raining. (If you need some more guidance, here are eight tips to cultivate an attitude of gratitude.).

“I want to thank my chosen family who made this workplace so special. Your support, humor, and occasional emergency snack stashes got me through some tough days and made the good ones even better.”.

“Thanks to everyone who made me feel welcome, challenged, and appreciated. You’re the reason I stayed as long as I did. Well, that, and Barbara’s famous cheesecake. I’ll miss you all (almost as much as I’ll miss all the cake).”.

Recent findings suggest that “A heartfelt thank you to my team — you made me better every day. I’m so lucky I got to be a player on this incredible squad. Rooting for all of you always. Can’t wait to hear about all that you accomplish.”.

In a recent development, A little story can go a long way. In addition to reminding people of the good times, it can make your message feel more original. You don’t have to write a novel, and it doesn’t need to be profound — just aim for real.

In a recent development, “I’ll never forget the power outage of 2019 when we all played trashcan basketball while waiting for the lights to come back on. We made the best out of a tough situation, and that speaks to the type of amazing people you are. Please stay in touch!”.

“Monday mornings just won’t be the same without our doughnut runs. Thanks for the memories, team.”.

Recent findings suggest that let people know all that you’ve learned while working and what you’ll carry forward. Not only will this help fill up your cup, but it can also remind people what they’ve learned while working with you. (Here are 20 questions to help with any potential writer’s block.).

It has been revealed that “This job taught me a lot about leadership, teamwork, and that I don’t need to talk louder while I’m on zoom. (Still working on that one…) But most of all, it reminded me how amazing it is to work with such loyal, thoughtful people. I’ll never forget it. Thank you.”.

“Beyond the spreadsheets and deadlines, I’m leaving with lifelong friendships, a few more well-earned wrinkles, and countless memories.”.

“This place taught me how to lead, how to listen, and how to troubleshoot a broken coffee machine under pressure.”.

Some words of encouragement, a simple goodbye, or even a little glimpse of what’s next for you can be a sweet way to sign off.

“I’m off to spend more time traveling, playing with my grandkids, and mastering the art of sourdough once and for all. Wishing you all continued success — and a little less time in meetings.”.

“Wishing you all smooth introduces, strong coffee, and at least one good laugh a day. Keep crushing it.”.

It has been revealed that “I’ll be around — probably in sweatpants, gardening gloves, or both. Don’t be a stranger.”.

💙 Consider listening to Endings with Tamara Levitt if you’re having a hard time saying goodbye to your work and the people you’ve met there.

It has been revealed that it can be tempting to sneak out, but saying farewell to your coworkers is a kind thing to do — and it can help you too. Here’s why:.

According to recent reports, 1. It gives you closure on your terms: Retirement can be a tough transition. One day, you have 50 emails and several meetings, and the next, your inbox is at zero, and you have nothing but time on your hands. Writing a goodbye message can help you mark the transition.

According to recent reports, 2. It opens the door for real connection: When you write a farewell message, you’re inviting people to respond. What better way to leave than by clearly seeing the impact you had on your coworkers?

Recent findings suggest that 3. It lets you shape your own legacy: Your goodbye message can be a tiny chance to shape how people remember you. Go out on a positive note — literally.

💙 Writing to a coworker who’s retiring? These retirement wishes can help you find the right words.

Industry observers note that an announcement and a goodbye note do different jobs. The announcement shares your news and your last day. The thank-yous and memories from the tips above can follow it.

Manager first: Tell your manager before anyone else, so the news doesn’t reach them through a group email.

Timing: If you can, send the announcement a few weeks before your last day so people have time to say goodbye.

Subject line: Use a clear one, like “My retirement news.”.

Opening lines: Lead with the news, then name who will cover your work.

Long tenure: If you’ve been at the company for decades, add a sentence or two about your time there, and keep the news first.

Sources indicate that here’s an example for someone who’s been at a organization for a long time: “I started here 30 years ago, and my last day will be March 31. Over the next few weeks, I’ll be handing off my projects to Marcus and wrapping up my open work. If you’d like to catch up before I go, please grab time on my calendar. I’d love to see as many of you as I can.”.

In a recent development, you don’t have to send a retirement message, but it can be one of the simplest ways to wrap up this chapter with a bit of closure and grace. After all, you’ve spent a lot of time with these people over the years.

Writing a short, thoughtful message can help you leave on a kind note. You might also be surprised at how meaningful even a few lines can feel, both for you and the people reading them.

There’s no one right way to send a retirement message. If you want to keep it casual, you could say something like, “After 15 years, I’m off to find out if daytime TV lives up to the hype. Thanks for the talks, laughs, and memories.”.

A more heartfelt message you could send is: “It’s been a true honor to work alongside so many talented people. I’m leaving with deep gratitude for my time here — and for all of you.”.

If humor’s more your vibe, you could say: “Today’s my last day. Thanks for the memories — and for being so nice about the fact that I was always muted on Zoom. You’d think after a few years, I’d learn my lesson, but I digress. You’re the best, and I’ll miss you.”.

Your tone depends on your personality and your workplace culture. If you’re in a very professional environment, a more formal message is the best way to go, but if your usual emails include memes and inside jokes, it’s okay to joke around.

In general, the best retirement messages usually sound like the person writing them, so trust your voice and just be yourself. You’ve earned the right to say goodbye on your terms.

There isn’t a standard checklist, but here are a few good touchpoints that can help you find your flow:.

Mention a funny or heartfelt memory.

Share a bit about what you’ve learned on the job.

Consider sprinkling in your future prepares.

Close with a simple and warm goodbye.

Yes. Email is often preferred in the workplace, as it allows you to reach everyone and provides people with an opportunity to reply.

Sources indicate that whether you send it to your whole team or just a few close coworkers, an email is a low-stress, high-impact way to say farewell. Just remember to hit “send” before IT cuts your access!

According to recent reports, if you’re retiring, your thank-you message to colleagues works best when it indicates who you’re thanking and what they did for you. You can add it to your retirement announcement or send it as a separate note.

Industry observers note that for the whole team, a few lines are enough: “Thank you all for the patience and the laughs. I couldn’t have learned this job without you.” If coworkers gave you a send-off or a gift, a short note afterward can say thanks again.

#10887. Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice

📅 18 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1568 w)
